Estimate the variance components of an LLM measurement system

Source: R/fit.R
msa_fit.Rd

Fits a crossed random-effects model to the parsed values of a study. Items, prompt variants, models and blocks enter as random effects; for numeric outcomes the interactions item:prompt, item:model and prompt:model are included by default. The residual variance is the repeatability (replicate-to-replicate variation under identical conditions).

Usage

msa_fit(
  runs,
  type = c("numeric", "ordinal", "binary"),
  levels = NULL,
  interactions = NULL,
  link = c("probit", "logit"),
  ...
)

Arguments

runs

An msa_runs object (from msa_run() or as_msa_runs()).

type

Outcome type.

levels

For ordinal outcomes: at least two distinct, non-missing, non-empty labels in scale order. For binary outcomes: two such labels, whose second element is the event. When supplied, these labels determine the coding regardless of the response's storage type. Labels require this explicit argument; their order of occurrence or factor levels do not determine the event.

interactions

Include the two-way interactions as random effects? Default TRUE for numeric, FALSE otherwise.

link

Link for ordinal and binary outcomes.

...

Passed on to the model-fitting function. For numeric outcomes, supplying any argument here selects a direct lme4::lmer() call on the original response, including when an argument is explicitly NULL. Expressions in subset, weights and offset can use the internal columns item, prompt, model, block and y. Row-based arguments refer to the rows remaining after missing or unreadable responses are removed. Other symbols in these expressions are looked up in the immediate caller of msa_fit(), as in a direct lmer() call; a wrapper forwarding ... must make them available in that frame. Other arguments retain their original argument environments when forwarded.

Value

An object of class msa_fit: a list with the fitted model, the variance-component table vc (source, variance), the model formula, the analysed data, counts n, the outcome type, and a singular flag (a variance estimated at zero, common with few prompt or model levels; the point estimate is still valid but its uncertainty is large, see msa_boot() and msa_plan()), plus numeric fitting diagnostics numerics (NULL for other outcome types), logical converged, and derived (sources estimated from two fixed levels, also in attr(vc, "derived")).

Details

  • type = "numeric": linear mixed model fitted by REML, returned as an lme4::lmer() model. See the numeric fitting details below.

  • type = "ordinal": cumulative link mixed model with ordinal::clmm(). Variance components live on the latent scale, where the residual variance is fixed (1 for the probit link, pi^2/3 for the logit link). Interactions are off by default because they are costly in clmm.

  • type = "binary": generalised linear mixed model with lme4::glmer() and the same latent-scale convention.

Factors with a single level (for example one model only) are dropped from the model automatically. For ordinal outcomes ordinal::clmm requires more than two levels per random-effect factor; a factor with exactly two levels (two models, two blocks) therefore enters as a fixed effect and its variance component is derived from the estimated difference beta by the range method (beta^2 / 2). This substitute does not subtract the AIAG handbook correction EV^2 / (n * r). It has positive bias: E[beta-hat^2 / 2] = sigma^2 + Var(beta-hat) / 2. Every such fit warns and both print methods identify the derived sources. The two_level simulation study and its table in vignette("validation") (vignettes/validation.Rmd) investigate that bias. Short runs establish reproducibility; quantitative findings require the full simulation runs. With fewer than three ordinal items the error is "At least three items are needed for ordinal outcomes."

With no arguments in ..., the numeric fit preserves the input doubles and conditions their differences before solving for variance ratios. Eligible balanced designs use a closed expected-mean-square solution. Unbalanced designs and multi-factor variance boundaries use an analytic profiled REML score and Hessian, initialized by lmer, with nonnegative variance constraints. A boundary solution re-estimates the remaining components. The resulting lme4 model retains the original response scale, row order and factor labels; vc is extracted from its VarCorr().

The numerics field records the method ("closed_form", "analytic_reml" or "lmer") and, for the default path, conditioning, initialization diagnostics, active zero constraints and convergence norms. Its input_rows maps the rows actually analysed by the model to the input, including exclusions by subset or na.action. The returned data and all counts in n describe those same rows. Initialization warnings are retained in numerics$start$warnings after successful analytic completion, and emitted if completion fails. Final-model convergence checks remain active. Explicit lme4 arguments retain lme4 warnings and errors. Initialization failures on the default path identify the fitting stage and retain the underlying engine's message. Numerical warnings or errors during original-scale model construction produce a named representability error. Final checkConv warnings can precede that error when the model is not representable at working precision.

Default numeric models store ordinary nloptwrap refit control with no extra optimizer options. msa_boot() and lme4::refit() therefore use normal lme4 optimization; they do not repeat the initial analytic completion. The actual initial method is also recorded in the model's optinfo$completion. Both numeric paths store the fitting data and evaluated arguments in the model call so it remains usable outside the original caller's scope. Printing or deparsing that embedded lme4 call can therefore be lengthy; printing the msa_fit object gives the compact study summary.

Constant numeric responses, non-finite values, non-identifiable components and a degenerate residual variance produce named errors. There is no absolute variance cutoff for small representable variation or tied scores. A positive residual variance does not guarantee a fit: with high repeatability, initialization, analytic completion or construction of the original-scale model can fail at working precision. Final convergence checks use the standard-deviation-ratio scale: a numerically singular Hessian warning can occur even for an identifiable balanced model with a closed-form solution. Numeric NaN and the string "NaN" are treated as missing responses, without a parsing warning. Missing numeric grouping values are rejected on both fitting paths. The default path rejects variances whose original-scale representation or model arithmetic loses working precision; conditioning cannot recover digits lost in the inputs.

Ordinal and binary fits discard missing responses, and labels outside levels, with a warning giving the count. All returned data and study counts describe the retained observations. Missing grouping values are rejected. No remaining response, or a constant response category, produces a named error. Binary numeric values (including numeric strings without levels) must be finite and exactly zero or one; they are never rounded. Row selection, including missing weights or offsets handled by na.action, precedes the choice of random and two-level fixed effects. Ordinal offsets are retained in data$.msa_offset and included in the model formula. Counts in n describe data rows; with ordinal frequency weights, stats::nobs(model) follows clmm and reports the sum of those weights. Non-identifiable two-level fixed effects and ordinal random-effect terms with fewer than three observed levels produce named errors. Before either latent engine is called, random-effect variances must be separately identifiable after accounting for the fixed effects. Confounded grouping factors, including interactions, produce an error naming the affected terms. This check includes the fixed latent residual variance: a random term with one observation per level, or a confounded linear combination of terms, cannot be separated from that residual. If all retained weights are integers, they count as multiplicities, including binomial prior weights for zero/one responses. Otherwise each positive-weight row counts once in this check, including the fixed-effect rank check. Zero-weight rows contribute no information. The original weights are passed to the engine unchanged. Weights must be finite, non-negative numeric values with a finite positive sum. Sparse covariance cross-products avoid dense level-by-level projection blocks when checking large designs. Ordinal singularity describes random effects only, not the derived components. Ordinal and binary estimates are invariant to row order and factor labels only up to the optimization tolerance of the underlying engines.

Without control in ..., ordinal fits use ordinal::clmm.control(iter.max = 2000, eval.max = 4000). An explicit control passed in ... replaces both limits, including when it is an empty or partial list. Optimizer options given directly in ..., such as iter.max, take precedence over the corresponding default limit, as in ordinal::clmm().

converged records the final engine diagnosis, independently of singular. For clmm, success means code zero for nlminb, or code one or two for ucminf; the matrix fitting path uses nlminb even if ucminf was requested. For lme4 models, success requires optimizer code zero and no convergence message other than the singular-boundary note. Missing or unreadable codes do not confirm convergence. On both numeric paths the final model decides: initialization diagnostics do not, and a final Hessian or gradient diagnostic means converged = FALSE even after analytic completion. Numeric warning behavior remains that of lme4 and its final convergence check. Ordinal and binary non-convergence is warned, including a diagnosis stored by the engine without an emitted warning. A range-method warning alone does not indicate non-convergence.

Known limitations

Zero-weight rows still contribute levels when selecting random versus two-level fixed effects. An ordinal fit can therefore reject a random factor with fewer than three levels among its positive-weight rows. Use subset to exclude those rows when that is the intended design. Numeric fits with explicit arguments in ... use lme4's diagnostics; the default numeric path's identifiability check does not apply to them.

See also

msa_grr() to turn the variance components into gauge R&R statistics.

Examples

fit <- msa_fit(ic50_demo, type = "numeric")
fit
#> Variance components of an LLM measurement system (numeric outcome)
#>   formula: y ~ 1 + (1 | item) + (1 | prompt) + (1 | model) + (1 | block) +     (1 | item:prompt) + (1 | item:model) + (1 | prompt:model)
#>   40 items x 3 prompts x 3 models x 2 block(s); 2152 observations; 2-3 valid replicates per cell
#>        source variance     sd    pct
#>    item:model   0.0053 0.0731  0.5 %
#>   item:prompt   0.0001 0.0092  0.0 %
#>          item   0.9672 0.9835 95.8 %
#>  prompt:model   0.0000 0.0046  0.0 %
#>         model   0.0171 0.1309  1.7 %
#>        prompt   0.0049 0.0697  0.5 %
#>         block   0.0010 0.0319  0.1 %
#>      Residual   0.0140 0.1184  1.4 %
# \donttest{
fit_ord <- msa_fit(acmg_demo, type = "ordinal",
                   levels = c("B", "LB", "VUS", "LP", "P"))
#> Warning: 12 missing response(s) were dropped.
fit_ord$vc
#>     source   variance
#> 1     item 9.25609132
#> 2   prompt 0.03887219
#> 3    model 0.27811382
#> 4 Residual 1.00000000
# }
